tagline: A short, carefully told story of famine, loss, and loyal love, in which a Moabite widow becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
overview:
Ruth is a four-chapter story set “In the days when the judges ruled” (1:1), the same dark period as the book of Judges, but told from inside one family in the small town of Bethlehem. A famine drives Elimelech, his wife Naomi, and their two sons across the Jordan to Moab. The men die there. Naomi turns home with nothing, and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her, binding herself to Naomi, to her people, and to her God. Back in Bethlehem, Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband, and through his generosity and a daring night visit to the threshing floor, Boaz becomes the family's redeemer. He marries Ruth, buys back the family land, and a son is born to carry on the dead man's name.

The book ends with a surprise that changes how the whole story reads. The child, Obed, is the grandfather of David, Israel's great king. A story that looked private and small (two widows, a field, a legal hearing at the town gate) turns out to be the hinge between the chaos of the judges and the coming of the monarchy.

Ruth matters for more than its ending. It shows ordinary people living out covenant loyalty (the Hebrew word is hesed, steadfast love that goes beyond what duty requires) in a time when Israel's leaders mostly did not. It shows God at work without a single miracle, through a harvest, a chance turn into the right field, and the choices of faithful people. And it places a foreign woman from a despised nation at the root of Israel's royal line.
author: The book doesn't name its author. The Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 14b-15a), a collection of Jewish rabbinic teaching completed around AD 500, records the tradition that Samuel wrote it, along with Judges and his own book. Most scholars today, including many who hold a high view of Scripture, doubt that attribution, mainly because the genealogy reaches David and Samuel died before David became king. Some scholars have suggested that the book's sympathetic focus on women's voices and concerns points to a female author or to stories told among women; others think that goes beyond the evidence. The honest answer is that the writer is unknown, a skilled storyteller who knew Israel's laws, customs, and older traditions well.
date: The story is set in the period of the judges, roughly the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC, but the book was written later: 4:7 explains a custom from “former times in Israel,” and the genealogy ends with David. Beyond that, scholars divide. Many date the book to the monarchy, perhaps in the time of David or Solomon (tenth century BC) or somewhat after, arguing that its interest in David's ancestry makes most sense while the Davidic house was being established, and pointing to features of its Hebrew they take as early. Others date it after the exile, in the Persian period (fifth or fourth century BC), and read it alongside Ezra and Nehemiah, whose reforms forbade marriage to foreign women including Moabites; on this view Ruth offers a gentler counterpoint. Scholars also dispute how much the book's language can settle the question, since some of its apparently late or unusual forms may reflect dialect or deliberate storytelling style. Both positions are held by careful readers.
setting:
The book moves between two places. Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judah about six miles south of Jerusalem, was a farming town whose name means house of bread, which makes the famine of chapter 1 sharply ironic. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, on the high plateau between the Arnon and Zered valleys. Israel's traditions traced the Moabites to Lot's son born of incest (Genesis 19:30-38), remembered Moab's king hiring Balaam to curse Israel and Moabite women drawing Israelites into idolatry (Numbers 22-25), and barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3-6). The chief god of Moab was Chemosh, named in the Bible and on the Mesha Stele, a Moabite royal inscription from the ninth century BC.

The story's daily life is agricultural: the barley harvest in spring (around April) and the wheat harvest that followed into early summer, gleaning rights for the poor, threshing floors, and the town gate where elders settled legal matters. Two institutions from Israel's law stand behind the plot: the duty of a near kinsman to redeem family land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25) and the custom of a brother marrying his dead brother's widow to raise up a son in the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). Ruth doesn't match either law exactly, and how the book relates to them is much discussed.
purpose: Several purposes are visible, and they don't exclude one another. The book traces the ancestry of David and shows that his line rose out of faithful kindness and God's quiet care, not from power. It sets a picture of covenant loyalty against the backdrop of the judges, showing what faithfulness looks like in ordinary life when Israel's public life had collapsed. It shows a foreigner embracing Israel's God and being received into Israel, which spoke to any generation asking who belongs to the people of God. And it treats bitterness and grief honestly: Naomi's complaint against God is not rebuked but answered, slowly, by events. In Jewish practice Ruth is read at Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, which falls at the time of the wheat harvest.
story: In Christian Bibles, following the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), Ruth stands between Judges and 1 Samuel. There it acts as a bridge: Judges closes with the words that everyone did what was right in his own eyes because Israel had no king, and Ruth closes with the name of David, the king to come. 1 Samuel then tells how David's kingdom arrives. In the Hebrew Bible, Ruth belongs to the third section, the Writings, as one of the five short scrolls (the Megillot) read at the festivals; in many printed Hebrew Bibles it follows Proverbs, whose final poem praises a woman of noble character, the same phrase Boaz uses of Ruth (3:11). Either placement shapes how the book is heard. Ruth also looks back to Genesis: its closing blessing recalls Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel, and Tamar, another foreign woman whose unconventional action preserved Judah's line (Genesis 38).
christ: The New Testament names Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus: Matthew 1:5 lists Boaz as the father of Obed by Ruth, one of four women (with Tamar, Rahab, and Bathsheba) in that list, several of them foreigners and all with irregular stories. Through Obed, Jesse, and David, the line runs to the one Christians confess as the Son of David. Beyond the genealogy, the book's central idea is redemption by a kinsman: a near relative who has the right and the means to buy back what was lost and to restore a family that had no future. The New Testament uses the same language of Christ, who shares our flesh as a true kinsman (Hebrews 2:14-17) and redeems his people at his own cost. Boaz is not a hidden prediction of Jesus, and the book doesn't present him as one. The link is a pattern that the rest of Scripture fills out: God providing a redeemer from within the family, and gathering outsiders under his wings.
reading: Ruth is a narrative told with great economy and craft, and it rewards slow reading. Watch the dialogue, which carries most of the story, and the key words that come back in new settings: return, empty and full, kindness, rest, wings, and redeem. Notice how the chapters are balanced, with scenes on the road, in the field, at the threshing floor, and at the gate, and how Naomi's emptiness in chapter 1 is answered by the child in her lap in chapter 4. Notice, too, how God acts: he is spoken to and spoken of constantly, but the narrator describes him acting directly only twice (1:6 and 4:13). Common misreadings include treating the book as a simple romance, which misses its concern with land, law, lineage, and loyalty to the dead, and treating the threshing-floor scene as either plainly sexual or plainly innocent when the text is deliberately delicate and suggestive.

structure.title: Emptiness and return
structure.summary: Famine, exile in Moab, and three deaths leave Naomi without husband or sons. She returns to Bethlehem, and Ruth refuses to leave her, pledging herself to Naomi's people and God.

structure.title: Gleaning in the field of Boaz
structure.summary: Ruth gleans in the barley harvest and happens on the field of Boaz, who treats her with unusual generosity. Naomi learns that he is a kinsman-redeemer.

structure.title: The night at the threshing floor
structure.summary: At Naomi's direction Ruth goes to Boaz at night and asks him to spread his garment over her as redeemer. He agrees, but a nearer relative must be given the first right.

structure.title: Redemption at the gate and the birth of Obed
structure.summary: Boaz settles the matter before the elders, the nearer redeemer declines, and Boaz marries Ruth. Their son Obed restores Naomi, and a genealogy leads to David.

themes.title: Hesed: loyal, generous love
themes.body: The Hebrew word hesed names a love that keeps faith within a relationship and goes beyond what duty requires. Naomi prays that the LORD will show it to her daughters-in-law (1:8); Ruth shows it to Naomi and later to Boaz (3:10); Boaz shows it in the field; and Naomi blesses the LORD for not withdrawing it from the living or the dead (2:20). The book suggests that God's own faithfulness often reaches people through the faithfulness of others.

themes.title: Providence without miracles
themes.body: No one in Ruth sees a vision or witnesses a wonder. Famine ends, harvests come, Ruth happens to enter the field of Boaz, the nearer redeemer happens to pass by the gate. The narrator lets the reader see God's hand in these ordinary turns without forcing the point. Ruth is one of the Bible's clearest pictures of a God who governs the small events of ordinary life for his purposes.

themes.title: Redemption and the kinsman-redeemer
themes.body: The go'el, or kinsman-redeemer, was a near relative responsible for protecting a family's land, name, and people when they could not protect themselves. The word and its verb run through chapters 2 to 4. Boaz takes on the role at cost to himself, and the book shows redemption not as an abstraction but as a person acting to restore land, household, and future.

themes.title: The outsider brought in
themes.body: Ruth is repeatedly called the Moabitess, and she calls herself a foreigner. Yet she chooses Israel's God, is sheltered under his wings, and becomes an ancestor of David. The book does not deny Israel's law about Moab, but it shows the door of God's people open to a foreigner who takes refuge in the LORD, a theme the prophets and the New Testament develop.

themes.title: Emptiness turned to fullness
themes.body: Naomi leaves full and returns empty, and she says so bitterly. The book answers her lament not with an argument but with events: grain in Ruth's shawl, a redeemer found, a son placed in her lap. It treats grief and complaint honestly, and lets hope arrive slowly.

keyChapters.why: Ruth's pledge to Naomi (1:16-17) is one of the great statements of loyalty in literature, and Naomi's bitter return sets up the whole book.
The chance meeting in the field of Boaz shows providence at work in ordinary life and introduces the kinsman-redeemer.
The threshing-floor scene is the book's turning point, where Ruth asks Boaz to act as redeemer and he promises to do so.
The legal hearing at the gate, the birth of Obed, and the genealogy reveal that this family story leads to King David.

parts.body:
Ruth is the eighth book of the Bible. It has four chapters, and it tells one family's story ‘In the days when the judges ruled’ (1:1).

A famine drives a man from Bethlehem, his wife Naomi and their two sons across the Jordan to Moab. The sons marry Moabite women, and then all three men die. Naomi decides to go home with nothing. One daughter-in-law, Orpah, goes back to her own people. The other, Ruth, will not leave her: “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God” (1:16).

In Bethlehem Ruth gathers leftover grain in the fields of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband. He treats her with a kindness beyond anything the law required. At Naomi's bidding Ruth goes to him by night and asks him to take her under his protection as the family's redeemer. He does it openly, at the town gate, before witnesses. They marry, and a son is born.

The last verses turn a family story into something larger. The boy, Obed, is the grandfather of David, Israel's great king. A Moabite widow who chose Israel's God stands at the root of Israel's royal line, and Matthew names her in the family line of Jesus.

Ruth is short and quiet. No one sees a vision and no one works a wonder. Yet it is one of the clearest pictures in the Bible of loyal love, of a God who works through the ordinary turns of a harvest, and of an outsider welcomed home.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Ruth is set in the same years as the book of Judges, but it looks at them from inside one family in one small town. Judges ends with civil war, seized women and the verdict that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Ruth shows ordinary people in those same dark days keeping faith with one another.

In Christian Bibles, which follow the order of the ancient Greek translation called the Septuagint, Ruth stands between Judges and 1 Samuel. There it works as a bridge. Judges closes by saying that there was no king in Israel. Ruth closes with the name of David, the king to come. Then 1 Samuel tells how his kingdom arrived.

In the Hebrew Bible, Ruth belongs to the third section, the Writings. It is one of five short books read at Israel's festivals, and in Jewish practice it is read at Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, which falls at the time of the wheat harvest. In many printed Hebrew Bibles it follows Proverbs, whose last poem praises ‘A wife of noble character’ (Proverbs 31:10). Boaz uses that same phrase of Ruth: ‘a woman of noble character’ (3:11).

Ruth also looks back to Genesis. The prayer of the elders at the end of the book names Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel, and Tamar, another widow whose bold act kept Judah's family line alive (4:11-12). The story of one family is woven into the story of the whole people.

The book does not name its author. The Babylonian Talmud, a collection of rabbinic teaching completed around AD 500, records the tradition that Samuel wrote it (Bava Batra 14b-15a). Most scholars today, many who hold a high view of Scripture among them, doubt that tradition, mainly because the family line at the end reaches David, and Samuel died before David became king.

Some scholars have suggested that the book's close attention to women's voices points to a woman author, or to stories told among women. Others think that goes beyond the evidence. The honest answer is that the writer is unknown: a skilled storyteller who knew Israel's laws, customs and older traditions well.

When it was written is debated. The story is set in the period of the judges, roughly the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC. But the book explains a custom as belonging to ‘former times in Israel’ (4:7), and its family line ends with David, so it was written later. Many date it to the time of the kings, perhaps under David or Solomon in the tenth century BC or somewhat after, because its interest in David's ancestry makes most sense while his house was being established, and because of features of its Hebrew they take as early. Others date it after the exile, in the Persian period of the fifth or fourth century BC, and read it beside Ezra and Nehemiah, whose reforms forbade marriage to foreign women, Moabites among them. On that view Ruth offers a gentler counterpoint. Scholars also disagree on how much the book's language can settle the matter.

Careful readers hold both views. These notes take no side.

The story moves between two places.

Bethlehem lay in the hill country of Judah, about six miles south of Jerusalem. It was a farming town, and its name means house of bread. So the famine in the first verse is a bitter irony: there was no bread in the house of bread. The family are called Ephrathites, after Ephrathah, an old name for the town or its clan.

Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, on a high plateau of grain fields and pasture. The trip from Bethlehem would have taken several days on foot, down into the Jordan Valley and up the other side. The chief god of Moab was Chemosh, named in the Bible and on the Mesha Stele, a Moabite king's inscription from the ninth century BC.

Relations between Israel and Moab were strained. Israel's traditions traced the Moabites to Lot and his daughter, remembered Moab's king hiring Balaam to curse Israel, and recalled Moabite women drawing Israelites into the worship of Baal of Peor. In the days of the judges a king of Moab had ruled over Israel for eighteen years (Judges 3). And the law barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3). An Israelite family settling in Moab, and sons marrying Moabite women, would have raised questions for a first hearer.

None of this is a word against the people of Moab, then or now. The book that keeps calling Ruth ‘the Moabitess’ is the book that makes her the great-grandmother of Israel's king.

The story's daily life is farm life: the barley harvest in spring, around April, and the wheat harvest that followed into early summer; poor people gathering what the reapers left; the threshing floor where grain was separated from chaff; and the town gate, where the elders settled the town's business.

Ruth is told with great economy, and almost every scene is a conversation. Its four chapters move through four places: the road, the field, the threshing floor and the gate.

Chapter 1 is about emptiness and return. Famine and three deaths leave Naomi with no husband and no sons. She turns home, and Ruth refuses to leave her. In Bethlehem Naomi says, ‘I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty’ (1:21).

Chapter 2 is the field. Ruth gathers grain and ‘happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz’ (2:3). He protects and feeds her, and Naomi learns that he is one of their family's redeemers.

Chapter 3 is the night at the threshing floor. Ruth asks Boaz to spread the corner of his garment over her, and he promises to act, once a nearer relative has had his chance.

Chapter 4 is the gate. The nearer relative steps aside, Boaz marries Ruth, a son is born, and the women of Bethlehem rejoice with Naomi. A short family line runs from Perez to David.

A few words keep coming back and carry the story: return, empty and full, kindness, rest, wings and redeem. Naomi's emptiness in chapter 1 is answered by the child in her lap in chapter 4. The barley Boaz gives Ruth so that she will not go back to Naomi ‘empty-handed’ (3:17) uses the same word as Naomi's bitter complaint.

Notice too how God acts. He is spoken to and spoken of all through the book, but the narrator says plainly that he acted only twice: when the LORD ‘had attended to His people by providing them with food’ (1:6), and when ‘the LORD enabled her to conceive’ (4:13). Everything in between happens through ordinary choices and an ordinary harvest.

One Hebrew word stands at the heart of the book. It is chesed, often translated kindness, loyalty, steadfast love or loving devotion. It means love that keeps faith within a relationship and goes beyond what duty requires.

Naomi uses it first, as she sends her daughters-in-law home: ‘May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me’ (1:8). They had been faithful to husbands who were dead and to a mother-in-law who had nothing left to give.

Ruth then goes further than anyone could ask. Orpah does what Naomi urges, and the book does not blame her. Ruth refuses. Her words are a solemn vow, sealed with an oath in the LORD's name. In that world a people and its god belonged together, so to change peoples was to change gods. Ruth binds herself to Naomi's people, to Naomi's God, and even to Naomi's grave: ‘Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried’ (1:17).

Boaz shows the same kind of love in the field, and Naomi sees God's hand behind it: ‘May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead’ (2:20). At the threshing floor Boaz tells Ruth that her latest kindness is greater than her first, because she has sought a husband who can carry on her dead husband's family instead of a younger man of her own choosing (3:10).

The book suggests that God's own faithfulness often reaches people through the faithfulness of others. Ruth's words are often read at weddings. In the story they are spoken by a widow to her widowed mother-in-law. Their loyalty is family loyalty under loss, and it is stronger for that.

parts.h: Gleaning, the redeemer, and the dead man's name
parts.body:
Three of Israel's laws stand behind the story.

The first is gleaning. The law told landowners not to reap to the very edges of their fields or to go back for what had been dropped, and to leave forgotten sheaves for the poor, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. Ruth was a foreigner and a widow. But not every landowner kept these laws, and a foreign woman gleaning alone could be mistreated. That is why Boaz's protection matters, and his generosity goes well beyond the law. He tells his young men to pull out stalks from the bundles and leave them for her.

The second is the redeemer, in Hebrew the go'el. A redeemer was a near relative with the right and the duty to help a family in trouble: to buy back land that had been sold out of the family, to free a relative sold into slavery for debt, or to take up the cause of a relative who had been killed. ‘He is one of our kinsman-redeemers,’ Naomi says of Boaz (2:20), and the word runs through the rest of the book.

The third is the custom of a dead man's brother marrying his widow, so that a son would be born to carry on the dead man's name and keep his share of the land. The law described it for brothers (Deuteronomy 25:5-10).

Ruth does not fit either law exactly. Boaz is not a brother, and the land and the marriage are joined in a way the laws do not join them. How the book relates to these laws is much discussed, and these notes do not settle it. What the story shows is a man taking up a duty at his own cost. At the gate Boaz says he has taken Ruth ‘to raise up the name of the deceased through his inheritance, so that his name will not disappear from among his brothers’ (4:10).

The Hebrew verb for taking Ruth as a wife, in 4:5 and 4:10, is the verb for buying or acquiring, the same as for the field. That is uncomfortable for a modern reader. The verb belongs to the language of law and contract. It does not mean that Ruth was property, and the book's whole story says the opposite.

Boaz is introduced as ‘a prominent man of noble character from the clan of Elimelech’ (2:1). The Hebrew phrase can describe a mighty warrior. Here it means a man of wealth, influence and worth. Later he calls Ruth by a matching phrase, ‘a woman of noble character’ (3:11). The two are equals in the thing that matters most.

His first words in the book are a greeting to his workers: “The LORD be with you.” They answer in the same way (2:4). Faith shapes the ordinary speech of his household. The harvest was shared work: men cut the standing grain with sickles, women bound it into sheaves, and gleaners came behind to pick up what was left.

He notices the foreign woman in his field and asks who she is. He has already heard what she did for Naomi: how she left her father and mother and the land of her birth to come to a people she did not know (2:11). So he keeps her near his own servant girls, orders his young men not to touch her, gives her water from their jars and food from his table, and quietly tells them to leave extra grain where she will find it. At the end of the day she carries home about an ephah of barley, enough to feed two women for some weeks.

When Ruth comes to him by night, he could have taken advantage of her. He does not. He promises to act, tells her there is a nearer relative who must be given the first right, and goes to the gate the same morning to settle it before witnesses. The nearer relative, who will not risk his own estate, is never named. Boaz, who takes on the cost, is remembered. The book quietly says that faithfulness to God looks like this: noticing the stranger, protecting the vulnerable, keeping a promise quickly, and doing it all in the open.

parts.h: The night at the threshing floor
parts.body:
Chapter 3 is the turning point of the book, and its hardest scene to read.

Naomi wants to find ‘a resting place’ for Ruth, a home and a husband (3:1). She knows that Boaz will be winnowing barley that night on the threshing floor, an open, flat place where grain was tossed into the evening breeze so that the chaff blew away. Owners slept beside the heap to guard it. Naomi tells Ruth to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, wait until Boaz has eaten and lain down, then go and uncover his feet and lie down there.

Ruth does it. At midnight Boaz wakes with a start and finds a woman at his feet. She names herself and asks him plainly: ‘Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer’ (3:9). To spread the corner of a garment over a woman was a way of taking her in marriage and under protection. The same Hebrew word means a wing, and in chapter 2 Boaz had prayed that Ruth would be rewarded by the LORD, ‘under whose wings you have taken refuge’ (2:12). Ruth asks Boaz to become the answer to his own prayer.

Readers have weighed the scene in more than one way. The words for uncovering, for feet and for lying down can carry sexual overtones in Hebrew, and some readers think the narrator leaves a suggestion of seduction deliberately unclear. Most readers, ancient and modern, read it differently: a bold but chaste proposal, made in the only private place Ruth could make it. They point to Boaz's praise of her as ‘a woman of noble character’ (3:11), his care for her good name, and his refusal to act until the nearer redeemer has been asked.

Both readings agree on the main things. The scene is charged and risky. Ruth put her reputation into Boaz's hands. And Boaz answered with honor, not advantage. He sends her home before dawn with six measures of barley, so that she will not return to Naomi ‘empty-handed’ (3:17).

parts.h: A Moabite in the line of David
parts.body:
The book keeps reminding the reader that Ruth is ‘the Moabitess’. She calls herself a foreigner (2:10). And Israel's law said that no Moabite might enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3). How can a Moabite woman become the great-grandmother of David?

The tension is real, and the book seems to know it. Readers have answered in several ways.

Later rabbinic tradition held that the law applied to Moabite men and not to women, so Ruth's marriage was lawful. Others note that Ruth had taken Israel's God as her own, and argue that the law shut out Moab as a hostile people, not each foreigner who joined Israel in faith. Many modern scholars read the book as a story set beside the law on purpose, holding up a Moabite whose faithfulness puts many Israelites to shame. These views are not exclusive.

The tension was felt in Israel's own history. Nehemiah read this law and acted on it. The book of Ruth kept alive the memory of a Moabite who belonged. The Bible holds both, and the prophets and the New Testament move toward a people of God gathered from every nation.

What is clear is how the book itself tells it. Ruth's welcome is a gift from the LORD. The elders pray for her, the women of the town praise her as ‘better to you than seven sons’ (4:15), and she becomes the mother of Israel's royal line.

parts.h: Naomi's bitterness, and God's quiet hand
parts.body:
Naomi's grief is given room. When she comes home, the women ask, ‘Can this be Naomi?’ She answers: ‘Do not call me Naomi... Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me’ (1:20). Naomi means pleasant, and Mara means bitter. She believes in God's power, and she feels it turned against her.

The book does not rebuke her. It does not argue with her grief either. It answers her slowly, with events: grain in Ruth's shawl, a redeemer found, a son placed in her lap. ‘A son has been born to Naomi,’ the women say at the end (4:17). The emptiness of chapter 1 is filled.

Readers have also asked whether the family's move to Moab, and the sons' marriages to Moabite women, brought the deaths of chapter 1 as a judgment. Some, especially in Jewish tradition, have read it that way. Others note that the narrator passes no such judgment, that famine was a good reason to seek food elsewhere, as Abraham and Jacob did, and that the book goes on to show God's grace working through these very choices. The text leaves the question open, and so do these notes. It gives no reader cause to read a loss in their own life as a sentence from God.

God's hand in the book is quiet. Ruth ‘happened’ to come to Boaz's field (2:3). Boaz arrives ‘Just then’ (2:4). The nearer redeemer happens to pass the gate (4:1). The narrator uses the language of chance with a wink. In this book nothing is really accidental, and nothing is forced. It is one of the Bible's clearest pictures of a God who governs the small turns of ordinary life.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Ruth
parts.body:
The New Testament names Ruth once and Boaz twice, and it is wise to keep to the lines it draws.

Matthew opens his Gospel with the family line of Jesus, and he names Ruth in it: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse” (Matthew 1:5). She is one of four women Matthew names, with Tamar, Rahab and the wife of Uriah. Several were outsiders, and each had a story people remembered. Readers have suggested that the list hints from its first lines that this Messiah is for the nations, or that it prepares for Mary, whose pregnancy would also cause talk. Many think both are true.

Luke's family line of Jesus names Boaz too: ‘the son of Obed, the son of Boaz’ (Luke 3:32).

That is all the New Testament says of them by name. It speaks often of redemption, but it never names Boaz as a picture of Christ, and these notes do not make him one. The book of Ruth does not foretell Jesus. It tells how the family came to be from which, the Gospels say, he was born.

Ruth is Israel's Scripture first. It is a story of Israel's own faithfulness in a dark time, and of Israel's welcome of an outsider. Nothing in it, or in the New Testament's use of it, is a reason to blame or look down on the Jewish people.

A few habits will help a new reader.

Read it in one sitting. It takes about twenty minutes, and it is built to be heard whole.

Read it right after Judges. The same years that produced the last chapters of Judges also produced Ruth and Boaz. The contrast is part of the meaning.

Listen to the conversations. Most of the story is told in speech, and the key words come back in new places: return, empty, full, kindness, rest, wings, redeem.

Do not read it as only a love story. It is about land, law, family names, loyalty to the dead and the care of the poor, as much as it is about a marriage.

Do not read the threshing-floor scene too quickly in either direction. The narrator tells it with care, and the care is part of what it says about Ruth and Boaz.

Watch the outsider. The book calls Ruth ‘the Moabitess’ again and again, and it ends with her among the mothers of Israel's king.

And notice how the book ends. Judges ended with no king and everyone doing what was right in his own eyes. Ruth ends with a name: ‘Jesse was the father of David’ (4:22).

hard.line: Famine, Moab and three deaths: whether the family's choices brought judgment, and why the text leaves it open.
Ruth's vow to Naomi: what it bound her to, and why it is more than a wedding reading.

‘She happened to come’: chance, and the quiet hand of God.
Naomi's plan: bold, risky, and how readers have judged it.
The night at the threshing floor: what happened, and the two ways readers have read it.
‘You must also acquire the widow’: the language of buying, and why it does not make Ruth property.

words.line: In Hebrew go'el: a near relative with the right and duty to buy back family land, free a relative or take up a family's cause (2:20; 3:9).
The Hebrew chesed: love that keeps faith and goes beyond duty. The Berean Standard Bible also says loving devotion (1:8; 2:20; 3:10).
To gather the grain the reapers left behind, a right the law gave the poor, the foreigner and the widow (2:2).
The land east of the Dead Sea, home of Ruth and of Orpah, often at odds with Israel (1:1-4).
Bitter. Naomi, whose name means pleasant, asks to be called Mara when she comes home (1:20).
In Hebrew Shaddai, a name for God linked with his power. Naomi uses it twice in her complaint (1:20-21).
The Hebrew kanaph means a wing or the corner of a garment. Ruth shelters under God's wings (2:12) and asks for the corner of Boaz's garment (3:9).
A flat, open place where grain was tossed into the breeze to blow the chaff away. Owners slept beside the grain to guard it (3:2).
The town's meeting place and court, where elders sat and agreements were made before witnesses (4:1).
To keep a dead man's family line and his share of the land alive through a son (4:5, 4:10).
An old name for Bethlehem or its clan. Naomi's family were Ephrathites (1:2; 4:11).
The son of Ruth and Boaz, the father of Jesse and grandfather of David (4:17).

timeline.what: The days when the judges ruled, the period in which the story is set (1:1).
The Mesha Stele, a Moabite king's inscription, names Chemosh, the god of Moab.
Elimelech, Naomi and their sons go to live in Moab (1:1-2).
The sons marry Ruth and Orpah, and all three men die (1:4-5).

timeline.when: The start of the barley harvest
timeline.what: Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem (1:22).

timeline.when: Through the barley and wheat harvests
timeline.what: Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz, a season of perhaps seven weeks (2:23).

timeline.when: A night at the end of the harvest
timeline.what: Ruth goes to Boaz at the threshing floor (chapter 3).
Boaz settles the matter at the town gate before ten elders (chapter 4).
Ruth bears a son, the grandfather of David (4:13-17).

timeline.when: The 900s BC or later, or the 400s to 300s BC
timeline.what: The two main dates proposed for the writing of the book.
The Babylonian Talmud records the tradition that Samuel wrote the book.
Matthew names Ruth in the family line of Jesus, and Luke names Boaz (Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32).

teaching.mapNote: Only Bethlehem is drawn, placed elsewhere on this site. Moab, on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, is left off because it is not placed in this site's records. The map makes no claim about any border today.
